message.content: I'm sorry you're in so much pain. The exam shows your heart and lungs are under significant strain, so this is urgent. I suspect fluid or urine is building up in your abdomen because the catheter isn't draining. That could be a blocked or displaced catheter, or a bladder or bowel injury, and the pressure may be pushing on your diaphragm and making it hard to breathe. Please tell me three things. What type of catheter do you have, and why was it placed? When did it stop draining? Have you had fever, vomiting, or chest pain? Next I plan to check your blood counts, kidney function, blood gas and lactate, and to get a chest X-ray and a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis to find the cause.

Thank you, doctor. I had a bladder surgery where my bladder was removed because of cancer, and I now have a pouch made from my bowel that stores urine. I catheterize it through a small opening in my belly. For weeks it's been getting harder and harder to get the catheter in, so they put a catheter into the pouch to drain it all the time. It stopped draining last night, and I've been making much less urine since then. After that the pain in my lower belly got really bad, and my breathing has been getting worse and worse. I also have spina bifida (a meningomyelocele) in my lower back. As for fever, vomiting, or chest pain, I haven't mentioned any of those, so I'm not sure about them.

Thank you, that history is very helpful. You have a continent urinary pouch made from bowel, and the drainage catheter stopped working last night. Your urine output has dropped, your belly pain has worsened, and your breathing is getting worse. My main concern is that the pouch has become overfilled or has ruptured, so urine is leaking into your abdomen. That would explain the pain, the low urine output and the breathing trouble, because pressure in the abdomen pushes up on the diaphragm. Other possibilities are a blocked or displaced catheter with a very distended pouch, infection or sepsis, or a kidney injury from backed-up urine. To check, I'm ordering blood tests (blood count, kidney function, electrolytes, blood gas, lactate and inflammation markers), a chest X-ray, and a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with a contrast study of the pouch. Please tell the team if you develop fever, vomiting, or chest pain.

message.content:
Your CT scan with contrast injected into the pouch shows the cause. There is a large tear in the wall of your bowel-made urine pouch, and urine and contrast are leaking into your abdominal cavity. Free fluid is also present. This is a perforated (ruptured) continent urinary reservoir. The drainage catheter probably blocked, so the pouch overfilled and tore. Urine in the abdomen causes your severe pain and lowers your urine output. It also raises pressure under the diaphragm, which makes breathing harder. Your inflammation markers (CRP 361 mg/L, procalcitonin 4.7 ng/mL) and lactate of 4.7 mmol/L point to a serious infection or sepsis, and your heart and lungs are under strain.

This is an emergency. You need urgent surgery to repair or revise the pouch and wash out the abdomen. You also need drainage of the urine, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and intensive care support for your breathing and circulation.

Final diagnosis: spontaneous perforation of a continent catheterizable urinary reservoir with urinary peritonitis, sepsis, and cardiopulmonary decompensation from raised intra-abdominal pressure.

I could not file this through the admission tool because it isn't available in this session. Please pass this diagnosis to the surgical and ICU teams directly.

Oh no, that sounds really serious. Please do whatever you need to do to fix it. I'm scared. I don't understand all the terms, but I'm glad you found the cause. Will I need to go to surgery right away? Is there anything you need me to do or tell you before that?

I understand you're scared. I'll explain this as simply as I can. Yes, you need surgery very soon, and it should happen right away. The pouch has a tear, and urine is leaking into your belly. That won't fix itself, and it is making you very sick. The surgeons will repair or rebuild the pouch and wash out your abdomen. You will get strong IV antibiotics and fluids, and the intensive care team will support your breathing and circulation.

Nothing is needed from you right now except to stay as calm as you can. A few things would help the team:
- Don't eat or drink anything from now on.
- Tell them your allergies, especially to antibiotics, latex or contrast dye.
- Tell them all your medicines and any blood thinners, plus any past problems with anesthesia.
- Tell them about your spina bifida and your bladder cancer surgery. Spina bifida can affect latex sensitivity and anesthesia planning.
- Tell the nurses right away if your pain, breathing, dizziness or confusion gets worse, or if you have fever, vomiting or chest pain.

Your family can be called to be with you, and you can ask the team any questions before surgery. One thing to be honest about: I couldn't finalize your admission through the system in this session, so I'm asking the surgical and ICU teams to take over urgently. You are not being left alone, and the team will look after you.
